questions.prompt: A stock looks exciting because the company is very small and could grow fast. What defensive test is being skipped?
choices: Treat small size as safer because growth can be faster.
Ignore company size if the story sounds promising.
Require adequate company size because very small companies can carry limited records, liquidity, and resilience.
questions.explanation: Adequate size is part of the defensive checklist. Very small companies can carry size risk that overwhelms growth hopes.

questions.prompt: A company has a popular product but a weak balance sheet. What should a defensive screen do?
choices: Require strong financial condition because debt and liquidity still matter.
Accept the stock because a good product offsets a weak balance sheet.
Focus only on the product and ignore ordinary business setbacks.
questions.explanation: Strong financial condition is a defensive requirement. Weak balance sheets can turn ordinary business setbacks into shareholder losses.

questions.prompt: A stock shows one excellent year of profits after an uneven record. What is the better defensive response?
choices: Accept the latest peak because one excellent year qualifies the stock.
Require earnings stability across years because a single peak may not represent earning power.
Ignore earnings records because conservative appraisal does not use profits.
questions.explanation: Earnings stability across years is required. Erratic profits make conservative appraisal unreliable, and a single peak may misstate earning power.

questions.prompt: A stock is dismissed because dividends are seen as relevant only to income investors. What does the defensive checklist say?
choices: A long dividend record belongs in the test set because sustained payments indicate durability and shareholder orientation.
Dividends should be ignored because they do not evidence financial consistency.
Dividend records matter only when no earnings record exists.
questions.explanation: A long dividend record is part of the defensive test set. Sustained payments can evidence durability, shareholder orientation, and financial consistency.

questions.prompt: A screen rejects any company without explosive growth. What adjustment fits a defensive approach?
choices: Demand explosive growth because defensive stocks need glamour forecasts.
Look for some demonstrated earnings growth, since stagnant long-term earnings can erode real value.
Ignore growth entirely because moderate growth is never relevant.
questions.explanation: Some earnings growth is required, but not as a glamour forecast. Moderate demonstrated growth is the conservative aim.

questions.prompt: A stable company looks high quality, but the price to earnings multiple is excessive. What risk remains?
choices: Quality makes any P/E acceptable.
A stable company cannot deliver poor returns.
Overpaying can still produce poor returns because valuation controls return.
questions.explanation: Moderate price to earnings prevents overpaying for quality. Even stable companies can disappoint shareholders when the multiple is excessive.

questions.prompt: A stock passes an earnings-based valuation test, but price to assets is ignored as irrelevant. What is missing?
choices: Asset value is irrelevant to common stocks when earnings look good.
Moderate price to assets supplies a second guard because earnings can be temporarily inflated.
Only price to earnings matters because assets never affect downside.
questions.explanation: Moderate price to assets supplies another valuation check. Assets affect downside and appraisal when earnings may be temporarily inflated.

questions.prompt: A stock passes one famous metric but fails several other defensive tests. How should the result be read?
choices: Passing one famous metric is enough for a defensive investor.
The strongest feature offsets several failures.
The tests work as a group, so one strong feature cannot offset several failures.
questions.explanation: The checklist is cumulative. All tests work as a group rather than isolated proofs.

questions.prompt: A screen is criticized because it may reject some future winners. What is the defensive purpose of the checklist?
choices: Keep doubtful issues out, since a defensive screen first limits error.
Maximize upside by accepting every possible winner.
Replace exclusion with story buying whenever upside appears large.
questions.explanation: The checklist is designed for exclusion. Its purpose is to keep doubtful issues out, not to find every possible winner.

cards.front: Why does adequate company size belong in a defensive stock checklist?
cards.back: Very small companies can carry limited records, liquidity, and resilience. Size risk can overwhelm growth hopes.

cards.front: Why is strong financial condition a defensive requirement?
cards.back: Weak balance sheets can turn ordinary business setbacks into shareholder losses. Debt and liquidity still matter even when the product looks good.

cards.front: Why is one excellent earnings year not enough?
cards.back: A single peak may not represent earning power. Earnings stability across years is needed because erratic profits make conservative appraisal unreliable.

cards.front: What does a long dividend record add to a defensive test?
cards.back: Sustained payments can indicate durability and shareholder orientation. They also evidence financial consistency.

cards.front: What kind of earnings growth fits a defensive screen?
cards.back: Some demonstrated earnings growth is required because stagnant long-term earnings can erode real value. The aim is moderate growth, not a glamour forecast.

cards.front: Why does moderate price to earnings matter for a quality company?
cards.back: Even stable companies can deliver poor returns from excessive multiples. Valuation still controls return.

cards.front: Why use moderate price to assets as a second valuation guard?
cards.back: Earnings can be temporarily inflated, while asset value gives another check. Assets affect downside and appraisal.
